opening.headline: When you want to connect your app with Claude and entrust it with code work, you will learn how to distinguish what the connector and Claude Code are responsible for.
body: If you're opening Mail, Calendar, or Document Storage and pasting the same information into a conversation window, you might wonder if you can connect the app directly. On the other hand, when editing or organizing code, there are many files, so conversation alone has limitations. Connecting apps and handling code seem to be the same thing, but the tools used are different.

In this lesson, we'll first look at the connectors, Connectors Directory, and remote MCP that allow Claude to access data from apps and services. Next, we'll look at how the Google Workspace connector works, how it's approved, how to set up your organization, and learn about Claude Code, who handles the code. Lastly, we explain why different tools are used for document organizing and code refactoring.
objectives: Can explain the role of connectors and Claude Code
You can distinguish between general user functions and developer tools.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

screens.title: I want to connect with my tools and leave the code work to you.
screens.lead: We look at two needs. When you select each item, an explanation will unfold.

items.prompt: Request 1: I want to connect with my app
items.answer: Opening mail, calendar, and document storage and pasting the necessary information into the dialog box are repeated. If Claude could access these apps directly, it would save him the trouble of pasting.

items.prompt: Request 2: I want to hand over the code work
items.answer: Renaming functions and organizing their structure spans multiple files. Pasting files one by one into a conversation has its limitations, and requires a tool that understands the entire code.

items.prompt: Are both needs solved with the same tool?
items.answer: It doesn't resolve. The connector is responsible for connecting app data, and Claude Code is responsible for handling code files. They're both named Claude, so they just seem like one thing.

items.prompt: How should we think about permissions?
items.answer: When you connect the app, Claude accesses your data and sometimes acts under your name. So, you need to check how far you can see and what actions require approval.

screens.outro: First, let me think of the app I want to connect to.

screens.title: Think about it: The app you want to connect to
screens.lead: Read the questions and think for yourself first. There is no need to submit an answer, and when you select an item, the instructor's thoughts unfold.

items.prompt: Which of the apps I use every day would I like to connect to AI?
items.answer: Mail, calendar, document storage, messenger, and issue management tools are common candidates. The apps you open most often during the day will save you more time when connected. When thinking of candidates, also think about what information is contained in the app.

items.prompt: Does the app need the AI to just read or write as well?
items.answer: The risks are different from those that require only reading and those that require writing, such as sending emails or creating calendars. The more writing you need, the more important the approval step becomes.

items.prompt: What kind of work does it involve dealing with code?
items.answer: This involves directly touching code files, such as fixing bugs, implementing features, renaming, or reorganizing the structure. This task is different from app connection, so a separate tool called Claude Code is used.

screens.outro: Now let's take a look at what a connector is.

screens.title: Connectors, directories, remote MCPs
screens.lead: If you hover over or select an underlined term in the following article, an explanation will appear.

visual.alt: Schematic diagram of how Claude connects to external services through connectors
labels: only to the extent of my authority
Service not in directory = remote MCP server (custom connector)

data.text: Connectors enable Claude to access data within apps and services and operate within connected services. For example, you can create issues in Linear, send messages to Slack, or search files in Google Drive. The core principle is that Claude's Permissions are inherited directly from the connected service. is a point. You can see which connectors are available in Connectors Directory, and each connector's page lists its purpose, read and write capabilities, and scope of use. Services not listed in the directory can be connected via custom connector under Remote MCP server. Connectors can be used with Claude, Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and APIs.

terms.term: Permissions are inherited directly from the connected service.
terms.tip: This means that files, channels, and records that I cannot view in the original service cannot be viewed through the connector. However, custom connectors that use shared credentials will reach wherever those credentials reach.
This is a list to browse for available connectors. Each connector has a page describing its purpose, read and write capabilities, and scope of use.

A server hosted on the Internet that communicates with AI apps. MCP is an open standard created by Anthropic to connect AI applications to tools and data. In the past, MCP servers only ran on user devices.

You can connect Claude to an existing remote MCP server, or connect any tool to a server you create yourself. Free users can use up to one custom connector. You need to be careful because you may be connected to services that have not been verified by Anthropic.

screens.outro: Let's take a closer look at permissions and approvals through Google Workspace, a representative connector.

screens.title: Google Workspace Connector and Permissions/Approvals
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what you can do for each service, its approvals, organizational settings, and risk coverage.

tabs.label: Gmail
tabs.body: With the Gmail connector, you can search and read messages in natural language, write formatted drafts, manage labels and threads, and list saved drafts. Attachments access metadata, not content. By default, actions such as sending, replying to, and forwarding mail will have Claude ask for your permission before execution.

tabs.label: Calendar and Drive
tabs.body: The Google Calendar connector lets you view events, including shared calendars, create, edit, and delete events, find common availability times for attendees, and respond to invitations. The Google Drive connector supports working with documents and storing files. Claude can also edit Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides on the web and desktop together in a window next to chat.

tabs.label: approval
tabs.body: Send, Reply, and Forward are writing actions that are difficult to reverse, so by default they ask for approval each time. In Team and Enterprise, owners decide whether members can perform this action without being asked each time. Just remember that every write action comes with an acknowledgment.

tabs.label: Organization settings
tabs.body: On Team and Enterprise plans, the owner or primary owner must first turn on the connector at the organization level so members can authenticate on their own. If members can't find the connector, it may not be turned on in your organization yet. With the personal plan, you connect directly. If you want all members to use it at once, you need to organize your organization settings first.

tabs.label: risk range
tabs.body: Custom connectors allow Claude to connect to services that Anthropic has not verified, and once connected, Claude can access and operate on those services. Custom connectors that use shared credentials reach everywhere those credentials can access. So only connect to trusted services, and make sure your reach is narrowed to only what you need.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the tools that bridge the app, let's look at the tools that manipulate the code.

screens.title: Claude Code: A tool to take on code tasks
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what Claude Code does, how to use it, and how it integrates with other tools.

tabs.label: something
tabs.body: Claude Code is an AI coding assistant that helps you implement features, fix bugs, and automate development tasks. Understand the entire code base and work across multiple files and tools. Unlike the Claude app, which handles documents in a dialog window, this is a tool that directly reads and modifies projects containing code. That's why it's classified as a tool for developers.

tabs.label: Where to write
tabs.body: Claude Code is available in the terminal, as an IDE extension, as a desktop app, and on the web. In Terminal, you edit, run commands, and manage projects from the command line. On macOS, Linux, and WSL, run the install command and confirm the installation with `claude --version` in a new terminal. Afterwards, when you run `claude` from the project folder, you will be prompted to log in the first time you use it.

tabs.label: Account needed
tabs.body: In most environments, a Claude subscription or Anthropic Console account is required. Terminal CLI, VS Code, and JetBrains also support third-party providers. Pro and higher plans include Claude Code.

tabs.label: Claude in Chrome
tabs.body: Claude in Chrome is Claude in your browser, who looks at your screen, pushes buttons, and fills out forms. It is linked with Claude Code to create a debugging flow that is created in the terminal, checked in the browser, and reads console errors and DOM status directly by Claude. Teams and Enterprise allow administrators to turn extensions on or off organization-wide, and set whitelists and blacklists for sites.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the characteristics of the two tools, let's apply them to two tasks.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Document organizing and code refactoring tasks
screens.lead: The instructor explains why different tools are used for the two tasks. Select the next arrow to follow your decision.

steps.title: Reading two tasks
steps.body: Task A is to gather scattered meeting minutes in Drive, summarize them, and create a draft email. Task B involves renaming functions and organizing their structure across multiple files. Both can be left to Claude, but they use different tools.

steps.title: Step 1: View the target
steps.body: The target of task A is documents from Drive and data from apps such as Gmail. The target of task B is a code file. The first crossroads is whether the target is the app's data or code.

steps.title: Step 2: Task A is the connector
steps.body: When you connect the Drive and Gmail connector, Claude retrieves meeting minutes from Drive, summarizes them, and creates a draft email. At this point, Claude inherits my privileges, so he cannot retrieve documents that I cannot open. The final action of actually sending an email basically asks for approval, so the content is verified before sending.

steps.title: Step 3: Task B is Claude Code
steps.body: Renaming across multiple files is correct only when you understand the code base. Claude Code is perfect for this job because it allows you to see the entire project and work across multiple files and tools. Gmail or Drive connectors are tools that handle email and document data, so they cannot be the center of code refactoring.

steps.title: Step 4: Determine permissions and when to approve them
steps.body: Either way, before you begin, establish the scope of authority and when approval will occur. If it's a connector, check whether it allows reads only or writes, and whether the connector is turned on in your organization. If you're Claude Code, narrow down which folders and commands you want to handle.

steps.title: Step 5: Continuing Tools
steps.body: You can also use both tools together. When checking the results of code work in a browser, link Claude in Chrome to create it in the terminal and check it in the browser. The connector can also be used in Claude Code, allowing you to read issues in the issue management tool and fix the code. However, the more connections you make, the wider the access range is, so it is safer to turn on only the connections you need.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The conclusion is simple. When it comes to apps, it's a connector, and when it comes to code, it's Claude Code. Tools that handle app data are also features that regular users can use, while Claude Code is a tool for people who write code.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen why tools vary depending on the task, let's summarize the lesson.

screens.title: Summary: Apps are connectors, code is Claude Code
screens.lead: Let's summarize what we've seen so far. Read it while thinking about the connections you need for your work.

paragraphs: Connectors allow Claude to read data from apps and services and operate within connected services. Look in the Connectors Directory, and connect services not in the directory to custom connectors that connect to remote MCP servers.

The connector inherits the permissions I have from the original service. Write actions like send, reply, and forward in Gmail require approval by default, while Team and Enterprise require owners to first turn on the connector at the org level.
Claude Code is a coding tool for developers who understand codebases and work across multiple files and tools. You can use it in terminal, IDE, desktop app, and web.
By distinguishing between general user functions and developer tools, you can quickly decide which tool to use for each task.

Keep in mind the conclusion of the case that connectors such as Drive and Gmail are used for document organizing tasks, and Claude Code is used for code organization across multiple files. Either way, the habit of determining the scope of permissions and approval points before starting is the starting point for safe use.

Finally, we summarize the inspection sequence when the connector is not visible. If you're on a Personal plan, check to see if you've made the connection in your directory. If you're on Team or Enterprise, check first to see if the owner has turned on the connector at the organization level.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Custom connectors can also connect to services that have not been validated by Anthropic. Make sure the service is trustworthy and has the coverage you need before connecting.

glossary.def: This function allows Claude to access data from apps and services and operate within connected services.
It is an open standard way to connect AI apps, tools, and data through servers hosted on the Internet.
This is a list of available connectors, listing each connector's purpose and read and write capabilities.
A coding tool for developers who understand codebases and work across multiple files and tools.
This is the step the user confirms before executing a writing action such as sending an email.

misconceptions.myth: Once you connect the connector, you can view all data from the service.
misconceptions.fact: Claude inherits my permissions from connected services, so he can't see any files, channels, or records that I can't. Only custom connectors that use shared credentials have full reach of those credentials.

misconceptions.myth: Claude Code is a chat function for general users.
misconceptions.fact: Claude Code is a developer tool for code manipulation, reading and editing codebases from the terminal, IDE, desktop app, and web. General paperwork is handled by the Claude app and connector.
Custom connectors allow Claude to connect even to services that Anthropic has not verified. Before connecting, you must verify that the service is trustworthy.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Connectors bridge the apps, and Claude Code takes over the code work.
The connector inherits my permissions from the original service.
Execution actions, such as sending an email, are subject to approval.
Distinguish between general user functions and developer tools and choose the tool that suits your task.
